solar_storm.title: Solar Storm Detected
solar_storm.what: A huge flare on the Sun has launched a cloud of fast protons toward the Moon. For the next 2 days, radiation at the base will be dozens of times higher than normal.
solar_storm.why: The Moon has no magnetic field and almost no atmosphere. On Earth, both shield us from solar particles — on the Moon, only walls, soil and water do.
solar_storm.principle: Shielding works by putting mass between people and radiation. Dense, hydrogen-rich material (water, regolith, polyethylene) stops solar protons best.

onTrigger.label: Solar storm: +60 mSv/day inside the habitat
Severe solar storm: +110 mSv/day inside the habitat

options.label: Move crew into the radiation shelter
options.benefit: Blocks about 90% of the storm's radiation.
options.cost: Shelter life support uses +10 kWh/day. Nobody tends the greenhouse (half production). Electronics outside stay exposed.

effects.label: Crew in shelter: 90% of storm dose blocked

effects.note: A proton strike scrambled a circuit board (a 'single-event upset'): one system has failed.
effects.otherwiseNote: The base's electronics rode out the storm without damage.

options.lesson: A dedicated shelter turns a dangerous storm into a small dose — but only if you launched it, and it has a power cost.

options.label: Build a water wall around the sleeping area
options.benefit: Uses stored water as shielding: blocks about half of the storm dose. No water is lost.
options.cost: Needs at least 100 kg of stored water. Crew busy moving tanks: greenhouse at half output.

effects.label: Water wall: 50% of storm dose blocked

effects.note: A proton strike scrambled a circuit board (a 'single-event upset'): one system has failed.
effects.otherwiseNote: The base's electronics rode out the storm without damage.

options.lesson: Water is one of the best radiation shields because it is full of hydrogen. Real spacecraft designs put water tanks around crew quarters.

options.label: Put the base in safe mode
options.benefit: Powers down the greenhouse, oxygen generator and recycler so the storm can't damage them. Saves a lot of energy.
options.cost: No extra protection for the crew. No food, oxygen or water recycling for 2 days.
options.lesson: Spacecraft enter 'safe mode' to protect their electronics from radiation. It protects the machines — not the people.

options.label: Continue normal operations
options.benefit: Every system keeps producing at full rate.
options.cost: The crew receives the full storm dose, and electronics can be hit.

effects.note: A proton strike scrambled a circuit board (a 'single-event upset'): one system has failed.
effects.otherwiseNote: The base's electronics rode out the storm without damage.

options.lesson: Radiation dose adds up over a mission. A single strong storm can use up a large share of an astronaut's safe limit.

power_failure.title: Power Failure: Dust on the Solar Arrays
power_failure.what: A nearby rover landing kicked up lunar dust, which settled on the solar panels. Their output has dropped by almost half.
power_failure.why: Lunar dust (regolith) is sharp, clingy and electrically charged. With no wind or rain, nothing cleans it off.
power_failure.principle: A power system is only as good as its worst day. Engineers design for degraded performance, not just ideal conditions.

options.label: Send two astronauts outside to clean the panels
options.benefit: Panels back to 90% tomorrow and normal after that.
options.cost: A spacewalk adds radiation dose (+0.5 mSv) and takes the crew away from the greenhouse for a day.
options.lesson: Spacewalks (EVAs) solve problems fast, but every hour outside costs crew time and radiation exposure.

options.label: Let the cleaning robot do it slowly
options.benefit: No crew time and no extra radiation.
options.cost: Solar power stays at 75% for 3 days.
options.lesson: Automation saves crew time, which is the most precious resource on a mission — but it is usually slower.

options.label: Ignore it for now
options.cost: Solar power at 55% for 6 days while the dust slowly falls off.
options.lesson: Small problems left alone can line up with bigger ones — like dusty panels right before a shadow period.

water_leak.title: Water Leak
water_leak.what: A fitting on the main water tank cracked in the cold. 8 kg of water has already leaked, and it's still dripping.
water_leak.why: Temperatures on the Moon swing by hundreds of degrees. Metal expands and shrinks, and seals and fittings wear out.
water_leak.principle: Redundancy and spare parts turn a crisis into a routine repair.

options.label: Replace the fitting with a spare part
options.cost: Uses one spare parts kit (5 kg more water lost during the swap).
options.lesson: Spare parts are mass you hope never to use — until the day they save the mission.

options.label: Patch it with tape and sealant
options.benefit: Free, and usually slows the leak a lot.
options.cost: Still loses 4% of stored water per day for 2 days. Might fail.

effects.note: The patch didn't hold — the leak continues for 3 more days.

options.lesson: Improvised repairs are a real part of spaceflight — Apollo 13's crew famously built a CO₂ filter adapter from spare materials.

options.label: Close the valves and isolate the tank
options.benefit: Leak stops immediately and for sure.
options.cost: 20% of your stored water is trapped in the isolated tank.
options.lesson: Isolating a failed part protects the rest of the system — a key idea in spacecraft design.

options.label: Just monitor it
options.cost: Loses 8% of stored water per day for 4 days.
options.lesson: A slow leak compounds: 8% per day for 4 days loses about 28% of your water.

equipment_failure.title: Equipment Failure
equipment_failure.what: A pump failed inside one of your life-support machines. It has shut down.
equipment_failure.why: Pumps, fans and valves run non-stop. On the ISS, life-support parts are regularly replaced because they wear out.
equipment_failure.principle: Reliability engineering: every part will fail eventually. Plan for repairs and keep critical systems redundant.

options.label: Install a new pump from the spare parts kit
options.lesson: Carrying spares for the most failure-prone parts is standard practice for ISS life support.

options.label: Try to repair the old pump

effects.note: The repair worked — the system is back online!
effects.otherwiseNote: The repair failed. The system stays offline — you can try again from the Systems panel.

options.lesson: Being able to repair things on site makes a crew far less dependent on Earth.

options.label: Leave it off for now
options.benefit: Saves its power for other systems.
options.cost: No production until you repair it from the Systems panel.
options.lesson: Turning a broken system off saves power, but your stored supplies now have to cover the gap.

crop_failure.title: Crop Failure
crop_failure.what: A root disease is spreading through the greenhouse. The plants are wilting.
crop_failure.why: In a closed greenhouse, microbes spread fast through shared water. There are no natural predators to keep them in check.
crop_failure.principle: Biological systems are productive but less predictable than machines. Missions keep stored food as a backup.

options.label: Clear everything and replant
options.benefit: Healthy plants again, full output once they grow.
options.cost: No harvest for the next 7 days while new plants grow. Uses 10 kg of water to sterilize.
options.lesson: Restarting a biological system takes time — that's why growth time matters when planning food.

options.label: Treat the plants and hope
options.cost: Only 40% output for 4 days, and the treatment system uses +5 kWh/day.
options.lesson: Partial output is often better than none — but it comes with its own costs.

options.label: Shut the greenhouse down
options.benefit: Frees 40 kWh/day of power and 2 kg/day of water.
options.cost: No more fresh food or plant oxygen (you can switch it back on, but it restarts from zero).
options.lesson: Sometimes the best engineering decision is to cut your losses and redirect resources.
